missed_issues: Production applicability: internal (@ocelot) code cannot handle exceptions (§4.1). Any external exception terminates the run, so retries, fallbacks and partial-failure handling must live in external code. That is a material restriction for real LLM pipelines with flaky providers, and the review does not mention it.

The 30 LLM-generated programs gain much less than the headline. A 1.8x geomean over all 35 with 3.9x on the 5 human-written workflows implies about 1.6x geomean for the CaMeL/ViperGPT suites, which are compared only with sequential Python. SecAssistant was also filtered to programs that run without error.

Table 1 credits LangGraph, ADK and LlamaIndex Workflows with parallel map. Their 2.0-2.1x deficit therefore reflects structure-preserving ports, where loops stay sequential inside a node, not an inability to express fan-out. The comparison measures restructuring effort as much as framework capability. This sharpens the review's strawman_baseline note.
Per-workflow framework results appear only in Figure 7. The text gives geomeans, so per-benchmark effect sizes and the ReliableRagQA regression cannot be checked numerically.
No provider rate-limit, 429 or cost behaviour is reported as concurrency rises. Speedups of up to 10.8x at fan-out 20 assume unconstrained API concurrency.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats and with the P36 'mixed' stance. This is the batch's only same-model, same-calls comparison. Graph frameworks beat naive sequential code but lose to concurrent dispatch of the same calls. The outcome is latency only, with one model and no artifact. I would put relevance at 1-2 for a Java coding-agent harness because the subject is LLM-orchestration latency, not coding-agent workflow design.
